summary:
Tumbes stands under Peru's national framework: trans identity is not criminalised, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. There is no documented local mitigation for this border department, and the national restroom rule applies to public facilities including transport hubs, which matters because the bill was triggered by a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chávez airport.

On 20 February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya of Honor y Democracia and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with exceptions for custody, where medical attention is required, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, plus a ban on 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho called the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including ID checks, and noted there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms.

On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved and exempted from second vote the bill, whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', save for narrow listed exceptions. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights; IDEHPUCP's analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte argues the Peruvian provision violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on a stigmatising stereotype that implicitly presents trans people as likely restroom harassers while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

Enforcement reaches private life: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, and on television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'. The same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry; between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack; it was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, leaving Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law. Two protective developments are on record: in June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, and in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional after an activist legal challenge.

Speech and association are also constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.
tangentialFactors:
The Inter-American Court of Human Rights' Advisory Opinion OC-24/17, binding across the region, holds that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights, placing Peru's restroom statute in tension with its Inter-American obligations. The IDEHPUCP analysis of the law rests on article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights.

Peru's position on hate-crime law is an outlier in the region: after the 2017 repeal it became one of only three South American countries, alongside Paraguay and Guyana, without LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime provisions.

The Azul Rojas Marín case reached the Inter-American Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights and, per BBC News Mundo, stands as the Court's first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, giving trans litigants in Peru a documented regional precedent.

Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people, framing the April 2025 law's censorship provisions as part of a wider pattern rather than an isolated statute.
localsOnly:
Residents of Tumbes face the national restroom statute in everyday public facilities, with access determined by 'biological sex' and narrow exceptions for custody, medical attention, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities; LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho warns that in practice access may depend on security staff's personal judgment, including ID checks.

Local gyms and private businesses have enforced the policy: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that applied it.

June 2024 health guidance removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity, affecting how trans residents are treated in healthcare settings, and a July 2025 Lima constitutional court struck down an anti-equality decree after an activist legal challenge, offering a domestic legal route for residents challenging discriminatory measures.

Recorded killings of transgender and gender-diverse people in Peru totalled 54 between 2020 and 2023, with trans women most affected, and a 2024 report's co-author Gianna Camacho stressed that official figures are only a sub-registry.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Tumbes-specific enforcement data, local police conduct, or departmental government statements on trans issues appear in the source inventory; the absence of documented local mitigation is an absence of sourcing, not a finding that none exists.

The inventory does not resolve whether the April 2025 restroom provision has been challenged or suspended as of any date after the IDEHPUCP analysis of 15 April 2025, nor whether the July 2025 Lima constitutional court ruling on an anti-equality decree bears on the restroom statute.

Whether Tumbes's border-crossing facilities, including the Huaquillas crossing with Ecuador, have been sites of ID checks or restroom enforcement under the new law is not sourced here.
